SANTA FE, N. M., November 1.—General McKenzie received the following dispatch from Daptain Bean, commanding United States troops at Fort Canon Gallagos, near the Navajo reservation: "Captain Haines has just been here, and reports matters very serious. At Bloomfield a Mexican shot and wounded Eugene Blancett, who has since died from his wounds. Haines is justice of the peace and captain of the militia, but is powerless, as a mob wants to hang the Mexican. About 150 armed Mexicans are present to protect the Mexican. Serious trouble is apprehended."

General McKensie immediately turned the dispatch over to Governor Sheldon, who at once ordered Colonel Max Frost, of the Second regiment volunteer guards, to proceed to Bloomfield and protect the prisoner with a company of militia, but before Golonel Frost could start, another dispatch was received by General McKenzie and Governor Sheldon, stating that the Mexican murderer had been taken from his friends and lynched, and that the mob had dispersed.

A SENSE OF DOUBT.

How is it that whenever you are thrown into the company of an unusually polite—an over polite—person, you almost m d e clydi u him? There comes to you acting upon the nervous part of you of which you know so little, a sense of doubt.

You are not averse to police bearing and manners—nay, you like them; you even find it pleasant to receive compliments so readily and glibly offered to you; to see the amiable smile; to watch the bowing head; and there is something in the scene of reverence and respect as expressed toward yourself very flattering to your amour propre. Yet in spite of all you are not sure of your companion's honesty. You are inclined to suspect that there is something cynical behind that smile; something hollow at the back of the compliment; something unreal in the look of regard. And you do not know in the least why you have this feeling, only you know you have it. At the same time you find it so agreeable to be made much of, to find your opinions suddenly of value (or assumed value) in the eyes of your fellow, that you hull to rest the spirit of doubt which rises within you, and resolve to believe your new friend an exceedingly polished and very delightful man. And I do not say he is not.— Home Journal.

A COAT OF TAR AND FEATHERS.
[Special Telegram to the Globe.]

GBAND FORKS, D. T., Oct. 27.—yesterday a man went to the school house grounds, hung around the outbuildings, and when the school girls came out exposed his person and made indecent proposals to them. One child told her teacher, and when she went home told her parents. Everything went along quietly, when several determined men signified their intention of treating him to a coat of tar and feathers. They went to the Griggs house and took him out of bed, walked him over to the railroad bridge where Thurber, the ravisher, was hanged, and told him he had but a short time to live. At last he partially confessed the deed, but that he did not intend to force the girl. He was taken to a quiet spot, his clothes stripped off him, and he was covered from head to foot with tar and feathers. He gave his name as Andrew Elliott, from Almond, Ont. He said he would rather take a coat of tar and feathers than be hanged. Nothing has been heard of him to-day. There is a feeling prevailing this morning that the man was not guilty but his confession stood against him. The principal of the school says he did not hear anything about it.

A PRETTY, THRIFTY TOWN.

[Correspondence of the Staunton Vindicator ]

One of the thriftest and prettiest little towns on the Chesapeake & Ohio Railway, is Alderson in Monroe county. The stores are large and well stocked and one of the largest is run by the grangers, who, strange to say, are still a very live and prosperous organization in that county, being quite numerous and well organized. They sell only and strictly at a profit of 25 per cent. and pay their dealers at the end of the year 10 per cent. dividend on their sales.

The lumber business is large and profitable, a number of new and pretty dwellings having been built, and a fine brige has been built across Greenbrier river by the counties of Greenbrier and Monroe, connecting the counties, which is a most advantageous local enterprise for the people in all that section.

The most noticeable improvement is handsome large three story hotel with ornamental mansard roof and 60 rooms, just erected by Messrs. Cogbull and J. W. Alderson. The house is well appointed, nicely finished and furnished, has a private table and is one of the most popular eating houses on the line.

charles-thurber-grand-forks-1882-10-24.A5:
A JUST RETRIBUTION.
The lynching of the negro Thurber at Grand Forks last night, is another demand for a law making the crime of rape punishable with death. There should be no limitation making the penalty only when a child of tender years is the victim, but it should apply in all cases and punishment should be swift and sure. That is the only way to protect society from the outrages which are worse than murder, and it is the only way to prevent such outbursts of popular indignation as that at Grand Forks last night.

Who is there to say that the people of that city did not act right and justly? They waited in a peaceful manner until the crime was fully fastened upon the brute and then hung him without judge, or jury. It is all well enough to moralize upon such cases and deplore the violation of law, and descant upon the peril of resorting to mob violence. But when a brute has invaded a community and committed a deed like that of the negro Thurber on Monday, every husband and father feels that the protection of his own household demands punishment swift sure and final. This is the one crime in the calendar in which lynch law is fully justifiable and the protections of society as well as the demand for more stringent legal penalties, requires that where the crime is clearly proven, summary justice should be administered. If Minnesota and Dakota desire to be relieved of such scenes their legislatures must pass laws fixing the death penalty for the crime and providing further for a special local local court, composed of the justices of the the peace or trustees of a town, who shall have jurisdiction to try and hang the offender without delay. There should be no delay or legal quibbles allowed to intervene. No change of venue, but on the spot where the crime was perpetrated, and before a court of the immediate community, the offense should be expiated. That is the way both to prevent crime and abolish lynch law.

Storming the Basile.
A TOUGH JOB.
The thing was settled. The rapist was not to be examined. The hanging was to come off immediately. The mob thought it had been guyed. It would believe no story about Mr. Bosard's desire for a few moments' delay, even if there was a way of getting a hearing. A knot of policemen and officers were in front of the jail. They were surrounded by the crowd, good humored for the most part as yet, and disposed to take things easily. It did nothing but yell ynd joke. The sheriff commanded order and called upon the law abiding citizens to quell the rioters. It so happened that all were rioters. No l. a. citizens showed up. The mob yelled. Cries of "Hang the ——!" were heard on all sides. They took it out in yelling, and there was a manifest need of a leader. It must be remembered that the vigilance committee did not have this move in charge. It was in favor of giving the wretch a hearing, and then lynching him. All the members of the committee who were on the ground attempted to quell the riot and carry out their programme. While there were many good men engaged, the most active of the men were railroad boys, friends of Burbank's, and those who went in for fun and a fight. They were unorganized and worked at a disadvantage. When Conductor Burbank appeared he was hailed as a leader. "We'll do as you say they shouted. "Where is he?" answered Burbank. "In there."

"THEN TAKE HIM OUT AND HANG HIM," came the order. Yelling and struggling, the crowd was unable to make any headway. A battering ram was procured and the mob opened to give it passage. It was vigorously worked, the officers resisting. The iron grating door was bent, but the wooden one behind it stood firm. A struggle unsued for the possession of the timber. The officers would steer it sideways and break the force of the blow. The crowd pushing in prevented good work. Little headway was made for some time. The lynchers became discouraged and took a rope, it was passed around the building, but just as the crowd commenced to pull, some officers cut it. Logs were procured for levers with the intention of tipping over the jail. There was a yell to set it afire, as there were a dozen kerosene barrels conveniently near. The idea was abandoned when it became known that there were four other prisoners in the building.

The longer the fight lasted the hotter it became. Men's blood was up, and they fought to hurt each other. Axes were brought into requisition, and several fights ensued in disarming men who wanted to chop something. The officers dropped men right and left with their billeys. Bricks were thrown; clubs were used, and many were the small injuries inflicted. In one scrimmage with Sheriff Jenks he was "held up" for the keys of the building. He lost them without being aware of it. He was borne off to one side of the building in a hand to hand encounter with two or three others, and while there the door was opened. A rope was attached to the bent and broken grating, and it was wrenched away. The passage was now clear.
charles-thurber-grand-forks-1882-10-24.A20:
THE GRAND FORKS LYNCHING.
The Negro Ravisher, Thurber, Hung With Hilarity and Dispatch.
The Grand Forks Herald has the following account of the lynching of Thurber:

Several men jumped in on the cowering negro. One pulled a revolver and tried to shoot him. He was restrained by a companion. The thoroughly dazed coon only said, "I'll go with you!" and started out. When it came to facing the blood-thirsty, wolfish mob, he faltered and hung to the bars. He was mercilessly thrust out and the noose thrown over his head. In vain he struggled with the desperation of a hopeless fight. The mob grabbed the rope and started on the run, dragging their victim along. A second noose was thrown over his head and in the confusion one party pulled one way, and another, the other. The negro never uttered a sound. He was perhaps half strangled before the mob found out its mistake. The lynchers then removed the nooses from his head and tied his feet, a large number then took the rope and started for the railroad bridge, the negro being carried. He was in a semi-comatose state, and presented a horrible spectacle. The bridge was reached at 3:45 without further incident.

On the bridge there was a delay of a few minutes, during which great crowds of people assembled under the bridge, and on the adjacent bluffs. The joking and jeering was still continued. One man yelled "Shove him in the river and save the town the expense of a burial." Not the first word of pity or even horror was expressed. Some yelled, "Hang him on the Minnesota side, he wanted to go there!" In fact a fine spirit of poetical justice and humor animated the lynchers and spectators. A call was made for Conductor Burbank and as he appeared above the crowd on the bridge, he was greeted with cheers. To him the satisfaction of arranging the noose under the left ear was granted, he being looked upon as the most befitting person for the job. That was done. The other end of the rope was attached to an iron brace. Then the body was shoved off the bridge, and a yell went up from the crowd. It was sent head first, making a dive sideway through the air, swinging and swaying like a trapeze performer. Before the pendulum motion had stopped, the negro drew up his hands as if in the act of prayer, and followed it by slowly drawing up his legs. He then commenced kicking wildly. His eyes protruded and his tongue fell out. Bloody froth oozed from between the lips. The sight was sickening and disgusting. Many turned away in horror, unable to endure the sight. Others laughed. The executioners on on the bridge passed around the bottle and drank to his health while the body was yet jerking. At four minutes past four he was swung. At thirteen minutes past four all motion ceased. At half past four he was called stone dead.

HUNG TO A BRIDGE.
Grand Forks, Dak., Oct. 24—After wiring von last night the particulars of the capture and interview with Charles Thurber, the negro rapist, the committee of citizens who had gone to Norton by special train returned about four a.m. They proceeded at once to the city hall, where they found the jail strongly guarded. Speeches were made by City Clerk Colling, Col. Smith and others advocating a postponement of hostilities until the prisoner could be given a hearing and proof of guilt established by witnesses. The crowd was about to disperse, when some one called out! "Hang the nigger!" "Let's hang the s—of a b—to-night!" etc. A raid was at once made and the outer doors quickly battered down. A lively tussle then ensued for half an hour, when the citizens again finally resolved to desist for the time being. Early this morning as the news was read in the papers, knots of excited men began to assemble about the city hall and discuss the situation, the prisoner having had time to reflect upon the enormity of his crime, and having had intimation of the fate in store for him. A Pioneer Press representative again called upon him just before the hour of noon, and found him sitting moodily in a corner of his cell, the remnants of an almost wholly untouched breakfast were by his side, and the anxiety of the day and night had told upon his appearance. He was evidently suffering considerably mentally, but responded quite brakly to the questions asked. He stated that he now fully realized the enormity of his crime and was still at a loss to account for the motive which prompted him. He still insisted that he did not succeed in his lecherous attempt upon Mrs. Burbank, but that the failure was due to his physical inability. In reply as to what he thought was in store for him he said he believed the people meant to take his life, and that if he must die he supposed he must, but he would greatly prefer imprisonment for life. He said that he believed such a sentence would be more than justice, and that he should plead guilty and appeal to the court and to the people to spare his life. It was generally understood that the prisoner would have a preliminary examination at the court house at two o'clock p. m. At 12:30 two hundred people had congregated in front of the jail to see him removed. At two o'clock the crowd had increased to five hundred and at 2:50 to one thousand. The crowd was quiet, but moved about uneasily. A rope was produced and deposited at the foot of a telegraph pole. At 2:50 Sheriff Jenks appeared with a warrant, and with the aid of numerous deputies conducted the prisoner to the county jail, where, by strategy in avoiding the mob, he was finally locked up. The crowd had filed into the court room, and being disappointed, went to the jail and demanded the prisoner. The officers beat them back and rendered powerless the battering-rams. Conductor Burbank, husband of the ravished woman, having arrived on the train, cries of "Where is Burbank?" were heard. "We will do as he says with the prisoner." Mr. Burbank, with tears in his eyes said, "Take him out and hang him."

This caused a renewal of the attempt to secure the prisoner and threats were made of burning the jail and attempts to pull it down with ropes and batter it in with axes. After a gallant struggle by officers, the doors were burst in at 3:45 and a rope was placed around the prisoner's neck, who made a desperate resistance. Three thousand people had by this time assembled and there being no tree or pole near, the prisoner was dragged for many rods by the excited mass of people. There was much a surging mass that no one knew the fate of the beast for some moments. At last the cry was taken up "to the railroad bridge," and hence the mob hastened, a dozen men carrying the victim proceeded to the second span and crowds gathered on the banks beneath. One end of the rope was attached to the iron brace when again Conductor Burbank was called for, and was soon seen hurrying along the tressle work. He was greeted with cheers, and was allowed to place the noose around the neck of the doomed man. In a moment more, promptly at 4 o'clock p. m. he was swung off, and fell a distance of about twelve feet before the rope tightened. The neck was evidently not broken in the fall, and the man at once commenced writhing and convulsively twitching his legs and arms. This ceased in a few moments, and when thought to be dead the crowd gave three cheers and dispersed. The body was cut down at 5:30 and fell a distance of forty feet to the ground below. An inquest is probable. Sam Treadwell, editor of the Buxton Blade, arrived on an afternoon train and gave the first authentic account of the assault upon the German girl, about which less has been known than of the assault upon Mrs. Burbank. The name of the girl is Minnie Tepka, and she is but fifteen years of age. The fiend drove out from Buxton to the farm of her father, about three miles from that place. He found the girl at work in the field, and told her to come into town and cook for him. She replied she must first consult her mother and started for the house. When about a quarter of a mile from the house Thurber jumped from the buggy and violently attacked her by throwing her on the ground. He failed to accomplish his design, as the mother and the men in the field saw the affair and ran to her assistance. Conductor Burbank, when interviewed as to the condition of his wife, was too agitated to make further reply than that the case was as bad as could be. Her throat was swollen from the choking received, and her eyes, face and breast were black and blue and bruised. Mrs. Burbank has gone to St. Paul to receive treatment.

THE PROSPERITY OF TRADE. If the object of production and trade is to furnish human beings with the necessaries and comforts of life, the present year is indeed a prosperous one. The world's yield of the most important of breadstuffs, wheat, is larger per capita than ever before and is well distributed. Those countries of Europe which earlier in the season looked toward America for an unusual proportion of their supply of breadstuffs, now find that their own lands are to yield vastly be-
yond their expectations. This, so far from being a misfortune to us, insures low prices for cereal food to our laboring population who have been sorely embarrassed for many months by the cost of living. There is even a probability of some reduction in the prices of meats, as the corn crop looks better every day. Merchandise of all sorts goes from producer to consumer much more directly than for several years. No sooner had the new wheat appeared than immense shipments to Europe began, and the receipts of both wheat and corn at the primary markets of the West are now large and increasing. It is the same with manufactured goods. There are no large accumulations of cloths, iron wares, boots and shoes or any products of the mills, but the demand for all these articles is at least a fair average for this season. This characteristic is noticeable also in the import trade. The value of imported goods in United States bonded warehouses at the end of July was only $38,295,777 against $39,285,740 at the end of July, 1881, and $60,222,255 at the same period in 1880. For a few months past an increase has been in progress, but that is natural to a time when the farmers are short of money, and a marked decrease may be looked for during the fall and winter.

Nothing has happened the past week which greatly changes the business situation. The money market has, however, derived some relief from the decision of the secretary of the treasury to prepay without rebate the $16,000,000 of bonds due the 13th. This was a timely act, as there were evidences of an effort to create stringency. The disbursements from the treasury during this month and next will be an important factor, $42,500,000 being due during that time for bonds, interest and pensions. Another influence favorable to high prices for stocks is a decline in the rates for sterling exchange, removing the danger of specie exports. The improving prospects of corn have also strengthened the bulls. The reports of railroad traffic have as yet produced but a slight impression, but that they will impart vigor to the list within a few weeks at the outside there can be no doubt. For July there was an increase of 20 per cent in west-bound business over the corresponding period of last year. The anticipated rivalry between the Lake Shore and the New York, Chicago and St Louis is the weak spot in the market. Gould's purchase of the Hannibal and St Joseph road has made a decided sensation, but what its bearings on the rest of the list will be depends on the plans of Mr Gould and the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy railroad. There are plenty of rumors about new lines and new combinations but they are largely the inventions of interested parties. It is claimed that not only Gould but Keene and Vanderbilt are enthusiastic bulls.

THE ARKANSAS ELECTION last week was not in all respects a model, although perhaps upon the whole better than its recent predecessors. From some places come reports of good order and free voting by negroes, but in other sections there was more or less violence and bulldozing, and a specially flagrant case occurred at Helena. During Monday night the court-house, used as the principal voting place, was taken possession of and barricaded by democrats, who in the morning filled vacancies on the board of judges before opening the polls, in defiance of law, and then managed apparently with a view to fraudulent returns. Ballots were taken in through a hole in a door so arranged that the voters could not see what became of them, and a numbering arrangement, intended to prevent fraud, ingeniously evaded. This last move had been foreseen by the republicans, and was met with the use of "coupon tickets," by the aid of which a complete record of their voting was kept, and the appearance of this device caused an outbreak. Democrats seized the white republicans who were distributing tickets and directing matters, beat them and took the ticket-coupons away, and then a number rushed among the crowd of 1000 negroes with pistols drawn and so frightened the blacks that they fled. This was but an hour after the polls were opened, and very few had voted. The negroes did not return, few voted in other precincts, and the republican managers abandoned the contest. The special reason for the outrage seems to have been the fact that the district was strongly republican. Gov Churchill had declared himself anxious for a fair vote for the good name of the state, in good faith it is thought, and the republicans had been assured by local democrats that there would be no trouble. In previous years the certainty of violence had prevent republicans in the county from even putting up a ticket, the democrats were plainly determined that one should not be elected this year, and they openly justify their action by referring to abuses of republican management in carpet-bagging times.

If his conclusions are correct, he has furnished a strong argument for a reduction of the tariff on cotton goods. He declares it "fully demonstrated that 'the South can manufacture its own cotton 'much more profitably than can be done in England or the North.'" From $15,000,000 to $18,000,000 of the capital has been invested within about two years, and a number of new companies are now being formed, one in Georgia with $1,500,-000 capital. The prediction is made that a few years will see the investment doubled. The Journal of Commerce quotes from a recent speech of Congressman Russell of this state to show that 50 New England mills, representing a capital of $50,000,-000, have paid in the past five years dividends of a little less than 7 per cent a year. BULLDOZING IN ARKANSAS. [From the Detroit Post.]
"Blessed are they who expect nothing, for they shall not be disappointed." The Republicans did not look for much consolation from the election in Arkansas on Monday, for since the bulldozers took possession of that State in 1874 it has been carried by the Democrats, whenever any opposition at all has been made, by a majority averaging about one-fifth of the entire vote. It has been understood that they would easily enough elect all the State officers this year, and a Legislature that would send Senator Garland back to Washington for another term. It has turned out that Col. Slack, the Republican candidate for Governor, ran with unexpected strength in regions where he was best known, and that in some localities where quiet and fair elections were held the Republicans have elected a few county officers, and there is a possibility that the Prohibitionists have carried Sebastian county against license, in which event the saloons at Fort Smith—the only place in the county where liquor is now sold—will be closed up. The general result, however, is not different from what was anticipated.

It would seem that in Arkansas, if anywhere, the Democrats might get along without seeking to intimidate Republican voters; and yet the reports from Helena are laden with a most outrageous case of bulldozing. Gen. M. L. Stephenson, ex-Judge of the Supreme Court, telegraphed from that town on election day as follows:

"The Court House was taken last night, locked and guarded. This morning judges were elected inside. No one outside was allowed to participate. Side polls were prevented by the violence of armed men at the polls. Men distributing tickets were knocked down and driven away and the tickets taken from them, voters were driven off, and substantially no voting was done any where in the city after 9 o'clock. One colored man was shot at three times by a Deputy Sheriff. This so terrified the others that they would not try to vote."

Phillips county, in which Helena is situated, has a Democratic County Judge named Sanders who was himself a candidate for the office of Circuit Judge, and whose election depended upon preventing in some way a full Republican vote. As County Judge he arranged the voting precincts in July last, and put them in such shape that about 1,300 voters, of whom 1,200 were Republicans, mostly colored, had to travel ten or twelve miles to reach the polls, and then all vote at the Court House. Sanders also appointed as judges of election two live Democrats and a colored Republican who had been dead for two years. The vacancy was filled, not "by the voters assembled," as the law requires, but by a little family arrangement inside the barrier.

In 1878 no Republican ticket was nominated in this county, because the Democratic shot-gun policy prevented, and in 1880 again the Republicans prudently kept out of the field. Some weeks ago Gov. Churchill expressed a desire that, for the good name of the State, the Republicans should be allowed to vote, and it was partly on account of his assurance of fair play that the leading Republicans of the county decided to move. They give the Governor credit for good faith, for he took pains to sendover his Private Secretary and Adjutant General a fortnight ago to receive the assurance of the Democratic County Committee that no intimidation or falsification of returns should be allowed, and as late as last Friday he expressed his disbelief in the possibility of violence, and afterward telegraphed to Capt. Barlow, of the Phillips county militia, to be prompt in assisting the civil authorities to prevent disturbance.

The local Democratic managers, however, failed to keep the pledges they had so freely given.

At 7:45 a. m. the polls were opened, only two or three voters being admitted through the two doors of the Court House at a time. As they passed along the corridor they handed in their ballots through a small hole high up in one of the doors opening from it—so high that they could not see the ballot deposited in the box. The law requires the name of each voter to be written in a book with a number opposite corresponding with a number written on the back of the ballot. To prevent a tally being kept outside, the numbers used were not consecutive ones, so that no

body could tell, even if he knew the number that was put on a ballot, how many votes had been actually cast.

Doings of the Elements.
Chicago, June 26.—The cyclonic storm, which for the past few days has traversed and desolated this section, seemed to have followed no particular course, but to have dipped down here and there at points widely separated, as cities in Michigan and Nebraska, Dakota Territory and southern Indiana. While the ravages in Iowa have been most serious to life and property, the aggregate losses in other parts of the region are very heavy. Among the casualties which have not been already mentioned the following may be given, as indicating the general character and violence of the elements: At Osceola, Iowa, yesterday, Adam Miller and Wm. Lowe were killed by lightning. A severe rain and wind storm visited Albia yesterday evening, with accompaniment of thunder and lightning. Trees snapped off like pistols, and many pranks were played by the wind, but no loss of life is reported. The storm appeared like a cyclone. Trains are delayed in the direction of McGregor, Iowa, by disasters to tracks and bridges. Much damage was done on Saturday in the neighborhood of Sionx City and Malvern, in northwestern Iowa. Between Morrison and Round Grove, Illinois, 2600 feet of the Chicago & Northwestern track was washed away. The Chicago, Burlington & Quincy suffered even worse. West of Mendola, Nebraska, yesterday morning, a terrific storm gathered in Butler county, and swept southwest through Saunders, Lancaster, Cass, Elco and Nehama counties, doing the greatest damage in a belt 25 miles in width between Wahoo and Weston. Corn was badly beaten down in the southern part of Saunders county, and small grain was utterly ruined. Two houses were blown down. In Wahoo a two-story barn was carried fifty feet through the air. A herd of 125 ponies were swept by the storm eight miles southward, over fields and through wire fences. Not a pane of glass was left in the windows facing the west. The schoolhouse at Clear Creek was completely wrecked. One man was killed and five injured near Talmadge, on the Missionri Pacific, while seeking shelter under a freight car, which was hurled against them. Corn will be put back two or three weeks. Numbers of cattle were carried down stream and drowned near Lanesboro, Minnesota. Roads were stripped of bridges, and made inaccessible, and crops were damaged somewhat, hay most severely. One man was drowned in Uldapho, Minnesota, while rescuing stock from the floods. Hawkes's family were severely shocked by lightning, the little daughter remaining unconscious a long time. Great damage to wheat is feared. Roofs were blown off, and much other damage done. At Decatur, Indiana, the loss was $4000. Three people have been killed there by recent tornadoes. The loss in Indianapolis is said to be fifty thousand dollars. Telegraph and telephone wires are blown down. At Lafayette, Indiana, was a terrible waterspout, eight feet high, on Saturday night, which chased a train coming to the city for a considerable distance. It whirled rocks and immense trees along in its course, but spent its force before it caught the train. A severe rain rain storm did $10,000 damage to Chester township, Ohio. WASHINGTON, June 28.—The secretary of war has under consideration the case of Major-General G. K. Warren, now lieutenant-colonel of engineers, who was relieved from command of the fifth corps at the battle of Five Forks, Va., in 1865 by General Sheridan. Warren made several efforts to have the matter investigated, but without avail until 1879, when President Hayes appointed a committee of inquiry, Major-General Hancock as president. The committee completed their report a few months ago; and a record of the case was submitted to Judge Advocate General Swaim for review. A NEGRO PLOT
UNEARTHED IN ALABAMA.
A Conspiracy to Murder the Whites in Choctaw County-The Ringleaders Arrested-The Most Desperate of them Tried by the Community and Lynched.
MOBILE, August 21.—In Choctaw county, Alabama, on Tuesday, the 15th inst., a bundle of papers, disclosing a well organized plan among the negroes to kill the entire white population of that county, was found near one of their rendezvous by two gentlemen. The matter was laid before the Solicitor. On Wednesday, the 16th, a quiet meeting of citizens of Mount Sterling and Butler was called at Butler to consider the best mode of suppressing the intended outbreak and massacre. After discussion it was agreed that the following ringleaders, Jack Turner, F. D. Barney, Jesse Wilson, Peter Hill, Willis Lyman, Aaron Scott and Range West, to whom had been assigned the duties of leading squads to Butler, Mt. Sterling, DeSotoville and other places, and killing all the whites at each place, should be arrested and lodged in jail.

Their arrest was effected on Thursday, the 17th, without disturbance or bloodshed. The same day a mass meeting of citizens of all classes was called for Saturday to decide the fate of the prisoners. The plot has been in existence since 1878, and the conspirators now number four hundred. They have powder, shot and guns. They think themselves sufficiently strong to accomplish their fiendish design. Sunday night, the 17th of September, had been appointed as the date for its consummation. The papers further showed that this day was selected because then the white people would be at camp-meeting unarmed, and could then offer no resistance.

The meeting called for Saturday brought together about 700 persons, among whom were about 150 negroes, who, after having the papers read, by an almost unanimous vote decided that Jack Turner was a turbulent and dangerous character, a regular firebrand in the community, and that the public demanded his immediate death. He was accordingly hung at about 1:15 p. m. in the presence of the assembled multitude. The crowd then dispersed, and all signs of a disturbance ceased. Everything was quiet on Saturday night. The other prisoners are still in jail to await further developments.

THE SHAM CONSPIRACY CASE.
We see that the New York Tribune is as skeptical as ourselves as to the alleged Alabama negro conspiracy which was recently made the pretext for lynching a prominent colored man in that State. The more we reflect upon the story the more convinced do we become that there is not a word of truth in the statement given to the public. The strong presumption is that it really means a revival of the villainous system of force and intimidation which disgraced the South for so many years. Nobody who knows anything about the negro will believe that he is capable of conspiracy after this fashion. His character is in all respects averse from operations of the kind. If he would conspire a little more he would get on better at the South, but he allows himself to be controlled by white men who are too often vulgar demagogues. In the case under notice we have little doubt that when the truth comes out it will appear that the man who was hanged had been an influential negro politician, and that his influence was interfering with that of some of the whisky-sodden blackguards who think the country belongs to them. We believe that all the conspiracy was on the side of these fellows, and that they have in fact established a terrorism over the colored people, and intend to use it for political effect. We trust, however, that the Tribune and other Eastern journals will at once dispatch trustworthy correspondents to the scene of action, and bring out all the facts. Certainly it will not do to accept the cock-and-bull story of a negro plot which the murderers have put forward to screen themselves.
jack-turner-butler-1882-08-19.A14:
THE CHOCTAW HANGING.
An Alabama Colored Man on the Infamous Outrage.
To the Editor of THE REPUBLICAN:

Seeing in the papers of the 22d instant a telegram from Mobile, Ala., dated August 21, in which it is stated that in Choctaw County, in that State, a bundle of papers was found on Tuesday, the 15th, disclosing a well organized plot by the negroes to kill the entire white population of the county, naming as ringleaders Jack Turner, F. D. Barney, Jesse Wilson, Peter Hill, Willis Lyman, Aaron Scott, and Range West, all of whom were arrested and imprisoned, and that it was decided by an almost unanimous vote of 700, 150 of whom were negroes present on the occasion, that Jack Turner was a turbulent fellow and a firebrand of the community, and that the public demanded his death, upon which decision the said Jack Turner was hung, please allow me sufficient space in the columns of your paper to express my opinion of the transaction and the cause which induced it. In the first place I do not believe that the

NEGROES IN THE COUNTY OF CHOCTAW, or any other county in the State of Alabama, or any other State, are so vindictive or foolish as to enter into any such plot as the one named in the dispatch, to kill off the white people. On the contrary, I believe the story to have been put in circulation by the mob as an extenuation in the eyes of the public of the crime of the "deep damnation of the taking off" of Jack Turner, who doubtless was an active Republican at the recent election in that State, and as such was looked upon as "a dangerous character, a turbulent fellow, and a firebrand in the community," for which he was adjudged deserving of death. The public manner in which he was murdered had for its object the intimidation of other "dangerous char-
COURAGE TO OPPOSE THE BOURBONS
in the congressional elections to take place this fall in the State of Alabama, and to disgust the independent whites in that State with their colored allies, and to force them to abandon the Independent party and to act, as heretofore, with the regular Democracy. The time has passed when negroes had a sufficient incentive to kill off communities of white people. There was a time when they could have destroyed nearly the entire white population of the South with impunity had they desired to have done so. That time was during the rebellion, when all of the able-bodied white men were away from their homes fighting to rivet the chains of slavery more firmly upon their bondmen, having left behind them, in the care of these "dangerous fellows," their aged fathers, mothers, wives, and little ones.

DID THESE "DANGEROUS FELLOWS," in a single instance betray the trust reposed in them during those trying days to the South? No, a thousand times no! On the contrary, these "dangerous fellows" labored faithfully on the farms for the support of their masters at the front and the maintenance of their helpless families at home, caring for the latter with an affectionate fidelity unparalleled in the history of any people ever held in bondage with the near prospect of freedom before them. I ask, now that we are free, what is our reward for our fidelity to our former masters during the darkest period of their history. The answer to this question is not very creditable to the white people of the South.

FREED BY THE POWER OF THE UNITED STATES, the best efforts of our late masters have been brought into requisition to prevent our enjoyment of the fruits of freedom. Laws enacted granting us the ballot for protection are nullified for the purpose of keeping us by local enactments in a condition as abject as slavery itself. In proof of this, look at the penal laws of most of the Southern States enacted by the Democratic legislatures since their usurpation of power in those States. These laws are a disgrace to the age and country in which we live.

AS A CAPSTONE TO THIS SUPERSTRUCTURE of infamy they now upon trumped up pretexts hang us up without mercy, and proclaim to the world that we are "dangerous, turbulent fellows, firebrands in the community," and therefore nothing but our removal by death can calm the fears of the public. Against all such outrageous proceedings as stated to have occurred in Choctaw County, as a colored man I most emphatically protest, and will continue to do so as often as they may happen, and as long as I can use my tongue or am able to put pen to paper.

Wm. V. TURNER.

Since writing the above I learn that there will be a meeting of the leading colored Republicans of Alabama residing in this city at 1510 L street northwest, on Saturday evening next, at 8 o'clock, for the purpose of taking action upon the Choctaw outrage.

W. V. T.

A FIENDISH PLOT. Discovery of a Devilish Scheme of Negroes to Murder the Whites—The Leader Hung.
MERIDIAN, August 21.—One of the most horrible and cruel conspiracies ever entered into by the negroes of this section, came to light in Choctaw county, Alabama, just across our State line, near Butler, the county seat, on Wednesday, of last week. It seems that some white men were riding along the road leading to Allee's mill, near DeSotoville, and found some papers, which, upon examination, proved to be the minutes of a negro organization, formed for

BRUTAL DEEDS OF BLOOD.

Information was gleaned from the minutes found that it was the intention of the negroes to make a general assault upon the whites between the fifteenth and seventeenth of October, and that the organization was four hundred strong and four years old, having been called into existence in 1878. Every member had subscribed to the most solemn oath, and binding obligation to secrecy, and the conspirators were pledged to kill every white man, woman and child in the county, "from the cradle to the grave."

A notoriously bad negro by the name of Jack Turner who, in his communications to the organization, signed himself "Gen. Jack Turner," was the evil spirit of whom the conspiracy was born, and who, if his wicked scheme proved successful, was to be made the ruler of the county with a big salary. There were also communications from "Capt. Jessie Wilson" and "Capt. Peter Hill" among the papers.

THE PLAN WAS,
when the time came for action, to divide the organization into three companies, to be commanded by "General Jack Turner," "Capt. Jessie Wilson" and "Capt. Peter Hill," who were to take up positions in the Butler, Mt. Sterling and DeSotoville neighborhoods, and attack the whole county simultaneously, and slaughter every man, woman and child that wore a white skin.

This news was circulated rapidly over the county among the white people, who organized and armed themselves and went in search of the blacks who were planning to slaughter them. They soon came upon "Gen. Jack Turner," "Cap. Jessie Wilson," "Captain Peter Hill," Secretary Fred. Bouner, Limon, a preacher, and two other leaders, names unknown, and took them in custody to Butler, the county seat, where they were lodged in jail.

Saturday morning Secretary Bonner was taken from the jail by the whites and interrogated, and notwithstanding the proof was coulusive against him, he denied acknowledge of the conspiracy and affirmed with Christian-like sincerity his innocence. He was

TIED UP BY THE TOES,
while Rev. Limon was brought out

to tell what he knew. He didn't know anything at first, but under the refreshing and persuasive influence of the lash, applied vigorously to his bared back, he remembered and told a great many things.

When the minutes were read to him, he admitted that he had heard them read twice before in the meeting; that he knew the conspiracy existed; that it was the intention of the negroes to kill the people, take possession of the county and make General Jack Turner rules, but that he had nothing to do with it. He admitted that he had been carrying the call around and getting the negroes to join, and that when arrested he was on his last round, and that he was paid fifty cents a day for his services. He could not be whipped into telling where the books and other papers of the organization were kept. He denied all knowledge of their whereabouts; said he knew they existed, but did not know where they were kept. He said that one of the negroes asked in the jail the night before if the white people had found the books and other papers, and that Jack Turner spoke up and said:

"No, they are not quite that d—d smart."

After this admission and other conclusive proofs against him, it was unanimously agreed among the whites that "Gen. Jack Turner ought to swing." So accordingly he was taken from the jail, and between the hours of twelve and one o'clock in the broad open day light of the day he was

HANGED TO THE LIMB OF A TREE on the main street of the town.

There was a strong intimation manifested on the part of the people to hang the other six, but older and cooler counsel prevailed, and they were spared.

It is said the people were as quiet and cool as people well could be under the circumstances, and that the execution of Turner was as deliberate as if done under the forms of law.

All is quiet now, and no further trouble is likely to occur.

THE CHOCTAW OUTRAGE.
Indignant Resolutions by the Alabama Republicans Resident Here.

Alabama " Intelligence, Intellect, and Riches."
There is no change in the situation down South. In one sense there has been no change since the war. What I mean to say is that the intelligence, intellect, and riches of the South are still united as firmly as ever against ignorance, illiteracy, and barbarism. The white population, which embodies the first named attributes, is as determined as ever not to submit to the rule of an inferior race, goaded on and stirred up by selfish spoils-seekers and politicians. Northerners will be wrong to mistake the occasional independent movements of the Mahones, Lowes, and Chalmerses as a sign that the old feeling has subsided. These movements are isolated, and their origin would have never stirred had they not first been overboard by the old organization. They themselves left, they have willingly followed the suggestions of our enemies.

Senator Pugh does not, it will be observed, include among "the white population" "the Mahones, Lowes, and Chalmerses." All recognized whites are, of course, still in "the organization" (of the Bourbons). Now let us see how Senator Pugh's Bourbon constituents vindicate his statements:

The Montgomery (Ala.) Advertiser is a "regular organization" Democratic paper. It has never wavered in its allegiance to the Bourbon Democracy. It is good authority for Alabama news. It gave an account of the hanging of the negro Jack Turner by the Choctaw County mob at Butler at the time it occurred. On the 27th of August in giving a further detailed account of the outrage it said:

Jack's captains were more or less scourged. One was treated to the indignity of being hung up by a big toe and terribly tortured. Still he refused to "squeal." They all prefer death to giving up the secret it is morally certain they carry with them.

This is not a "Radical" campaign story; nor is it an "Independent" or "Liberal" version. It is the statement of the Montgomery (Ala.) Advertiser of the 27th of August. Indeed, we find it reproduced in that paper of a still later date, in an extract from a private letter to the editor, who says he publishes it by permission. The writer praises the Advertiser editor for the noble stand taken by him against mob law, alluding especially to some lynching done in Chalmers County. He then says: "And now I read, in your issue of the 27th instant, about the hanging of Jack Turner, this extract." Then follows the above quotation describing the torture inflicted on negroes to make them "squeal." Then the writer thus addresses his friend, the editor, who indorses the language in his introductory remarks:

All the captains were "scourged" and one "terribly tortured." He refused to "squeal." It is possible he knew nothing to "squeal."

These are terrible, ominous words to be flippantly used in this Christian era in this land. What more horrible can be said of Torquemada's inquisition? It smacks of auto de fe. It sounds like the cracking of human bones on "The Wheel."

"scourged," "terribly tortured," to make a prisoner "squeal!" Can such things happen in our midst? The crime was great with which they were charged. But our race has battled for a thousand years against the practice of "torturing" prisoners to make them "squeal."

Such torture, to-morrow, would make a hundred thousand innocent persons in Alabama falsely "squeal" out their guilt of atrocious crime to ease the racking pain. Can the law-abiding people of Alabama afford to allow this introduction of these measures as ministrations of justice? The press should unsparingly denounce and rebuke this lawless, cruel, demon spirit of mob law which is growing up in our midst.

The victim to-day may be an ignorant, friendless outcast. To-morrow, who can tell who the victim will be?

It is no excuse to say they conspired to perpetrate a great crime. There is but one way to find that out in a country of law.

The Advertiser does not agree that Turner was hung as a preventive of the too free exercise by negroes of their right to vote. On the contrary, it intimates its belief in the guilt of Turner and his as-
jack-turner-butler-1882-08-19.A32:
The Choctaw Outrage against Humanity.
ture of other leading colored citizens at Butler, Choctaw county. On the contrary as the facts slowly are revealed the whole affair assumes more and more the dark, forbiding and wicked aspect of a vindictive political plot, planned with attempted cunning by several leading Democratic politicians and defeated candidates in the late election. They inflamed the passions and prejudices of a sufficient number of the white people by thus basely exciting their fears and thus executed this diabolical plot and foul murder which has disgraced the State in the eyes of the world.

For further information to our readers on this remarkable occurrence we make the following extracts from an exhaustive and truthful review of the affair in the Mobile Gazette of the S.d.

We continue this article with the statement made to the editor of the Gazette by Moses Turner, of Choctaw county, now in Mobile, referred to in the papers purporting to have been found, as "Captain Moses Turner." He says:

On the morning of the 17th, there came to his house, Bill Curtis, Sid Prince and three other white men whose names he did not know, each armed with a shotgun. He saw them coming, closed the door, hid himself away, and instructed his children to say, if any inquirers were made for him, that he had left the place. Bill Curtis in
that nominated a candidate for the position of Governor of New York.

The statement that Fred Barney was nominated for the position of
white people, bears upon its face the impress of untruth, as Fred Barney is an educated man and not illiterate as these pretended records would show.

Governor Cobb, of Alabama, Denounces the Choctaw Outrage.

The following letter from the Governor of Alabama, by his private secretary, is a sufficient answer to the efforts of Northern Democratic editors to make light of the hanging of Jack Turner, at Butler, Choctaw County, Ala., on the 19th ult. It is addressed to the State's attorney for the circuit:

MONTGOMERY, Aug. 30, 1882.

Hon. George W. Taylor, Butler, Ala.:

DEAR SIR: The death of the negro Jack Turner at the hands of a mob in Choctaw County, the circumstances under which the lawless act was perpetrated, and the use that is being made of the affair, constitute an event of such gravity that the governor deems it important to have from the officers of the county charged therein with the enforcement of the law and the maintenance of the peace a full report of all the facts in the case. No other recent event in the State has occasioned so much regret at home or has elsewhere excited so profound a feeling. The peace and dignity of the State are offended, the good name of the Commonwealth suffers abroad, and the county is reproached wherever the story is told. The law provides adequate punishment for every criminal act and establishes all the necessary agencies for the administration of justice. Mob violence is lawlessness to be deplored by every good citizen and to be resisted by every conservator of the peace. The act under consideration, notwithstanding the provocation unofficially reported, appears to be an aggravated one, for the victim was in the hands of the officers of justice, and in jail would have been as powerless for the prosecution of the plans attributed to him as he is in the grave. He was murdered, and under circumstances that afford mendacious enemies of our people and section a pretext for attributing his death to political or race antipathies. The governor understands, of course, that your official duties in such cases begin with the grand jury and end with the petit jury, and he knows you will fearlessly and faithfully discharge them; but he hopes in the meantime, and promptly, you will take it upon yourself, asking the assistance of the county officers, to make a full investigation of the tragedy and report the facts to him. Very respectfully,

ROBERT McKEE,
Private Secretary.

The reply to this is addressed to the governor, and makes more than a column in the Montgomery Advertiser. It is addressed to the governor and begins with the words: "In response to your letter." It is signed by George W. Taylor, solicitor first judicial circuit; L. L. Belsher, county superintendent education; John A. Harmon, sheriff Choctaw County; B. H. Warren, judge of probate; R. A. Moody, tax assessor; Joseph Breitling, county commissioner; J. C. Chapman, clerk circuit court; and S. P. Smith, county treasurer. It is a defense of the sickening atrocity, and merely claims that the murdered man was dangerous. We quote the following:

Under the firm belief of imperious and impending necessity, they (the people) took the law into their own hands, and, as they believed, to save the lives of many, they sacrificed one.

They disdain to answer the governor's argument that the victim Turner, being in jail, was as powerless for harm "as he is in the grave;" but they show how deep his rebuke cuts into their sensibilities in the words with which they close. They say:

With the highest respect for your Excellency, we feel constrained to say that a judgment which results in such bitter condemnation as your letter contains might very well have been reserved until the facts had been presented.

Just for decency's sake, and in order to seem to be divided on the subject, some of the Democratic papers ought to take sides with Alabama's Democratic governor against the Choctaw County mob murderers.

The Murdered Deputy Collector.
DETAILS OF THE KILLING OF JAMES M. DAVIS BY MOONSHINERS IN TENNESSEE.

Deputy Collector James M. Davis, of the internal revenue service, who was waylaid and murdered by moonshiners near Nashville, Tenn., a few days ago, was one of the most valuable men in the service. The commissioner of internal revenue says he never hesitated to do his duty, no matter what the odds, and that he was as brave as a lion. He has long been a terror to moonshiners, and they have been trying hard to get him out of the way. About a year ago he had his hip broken and his skull fractured in two places. Commissioner Raum ordered him here at once, and he was under the care of Dr. Bliss for some time. He entirely recovered from his injuries, and since has done good work. His assassination is quite a blow to the internal revenue service. Although Commissioner Raum is anxious to bring the assassins to justice, it is generally believed in Tennessee that the reward of $300 for each is insufficient to secure their arrest, as all are regarded as desperate men, well used to handling firearms.

A gentleman, who arrived at Nashville from the mountains a few days ago, said that if Davis had had half a chance he would singly and alone have fought his assassins, eight to twelve in number; was riding without a saddle girth, which had been lost, so that when the horse jumped at the first fire he was thrown to the ground. He lay on the earth as if dead for a short time, having been hit in the leg. He finally got up and started back limping, when the bushwhackers began to fire at him and he again fell prostrate. One of the assassins then walked up upon the embankment and shot the top of his head off with a double-barrelled shotgun. Davis and his prisoner. Vickers, were allowed to pass the ambuscade before the murderers fired upon him. It was thought that this was done in order to get Vickers out of range of their shots. Davis, wounded as he was, fired three shots, while U. S. Commissioner Campbell, who was 150 yards behind, fired one shot. After they had killed Davis the party departed, taking a path leading over Ben Lomond Mountain, above McMinnville, whence they came. They were seen in the suburbs of McMinnville on the morning preceding the assassination and some persons talking to them. One hundred shots were fired. Twenty-six bullet holes were found in the back portion of Davis' coat.

Capt. Jas. M. Davis Killed.
Deputy Collector Davis and his men were returning from Beersheba Springs to this place Monday last, and when about three miles from here Davis was fired upon by some parties in ambush. At the first fire Thomas Vickers, who was riding with Davis, fled. When shot Davis fell from his horse, but soon regained his feet and started back up the road toward Campbell and Cathcart who were in the rear. He had not gone far, however, when he was fired upon again and killed. An inquest was held and the body was brought to town. Between twenty and thirty bullets were found in the body and the skull was litterally shattered with pistol balls.

The shooting was done by men concealed behind breastworks constructed of logs and cord-wood and covered over with cedar brush. This structure was about ten feet from the Beersheba road and the underbrush had been cut away so as to leave an unobstructed view. The assaulting party is estimated at from 10 to 15 men, George Campbell, who has been with Davis a long time, and was with him on this trip, states that Davis' conduct was very strange for two or three days prior to his death, that he manifested signs of restlessness and depression altogether unusual in him. Vickers states that Davis was laughing and telling a long anecdote when he rode into the deadly ambush and the shooting began.

Prior to his employment by the United States, about 11 years ago, Davis was engaged by the state of Tennessee in recapturing escaped penitentiary convicts and arresting horse thieves with which the State was cursed directly after the war. DAVIS' DEATH.
A Presentiment Which Made Him Restive.
It appears that Davis had a presentiment that he would be killed before he got off the mountains. In consequence he was restive from the time he left McMinnville. When he had reached a point not far from the ambuseade on the Beersheba road, Vickers says Davis called his attention to some loose horses on Ben Lomond mountain, but Vickers could not observe them. Davis had been to Beersheba and was on his way to McMinnville. His assassins had come over the point at Ben Lomond mountain. At one place on the mountain the road to the rear could be observed for a distance of two miles. When Davis and his men came in sight, on this part of the road, a pistol shot was fired. This was believed to have been a signal to the assassins that Davis and his men had come in sight, and for them to make all the necessary arrangements to kill him. The shooting did not occur until half an hour after the signal. Before reaching the ambuseade Davis got Vickers to get down and let out his stirrup straps, that he might simply touch the stirrups with his toes. The ambush was so constructed that each one of the eight men had a porthole through which he could fire, the base of it being a large log, with wings, made of cord wood, thrown out in front and on each side, and covered with cedar. It is believed the oysters, in the cans found, must have been eaten on some day previous to the assassination. It is said that in their testimony before the coroner's jury, two wood-choppers within fifteen feet of whom the assassins passed, denied having known the men. The white man testified that he thought he knew five of the men when they were approaching him, but he was satisfied he did not know any of them after they had passed by him. The negro testified that he did not know any of the men in the crowd and could not identify any one of them. They came upon him and his white companion so unexpectedly that he was scared and said to them out of fear, perhaps, more than anything else, "we surrender," supposing they had come after them, but why he could not tell. None of the men said anything, and went off in another direction.

It is thought that the two wood choppers, even if they had recognized any of the men, would not dare to say so from fear of the vengeance of the assassins or their friends. It will thus be very difficult to discover the men who killed Davis.

Some men are suspected of having taken part in the assassination, but it is doubtless whether the real assassins will ever be found.—[American.

A Sensation in Philadelphia — The Ghouls Nearly Lynched.

PHILADELPHIA, Dec. 5. — Frank McNamee, Dutch Pillett and Levi Chew, the latter a colored man, were arrested late last night while driving a wagon, containing five dead bodies, to a medical college. The bodies had been stolen from the Lebanon Cemetery, a burying ground for colored persons in the lower part of the city. The prisoners are professional "resurrectionists," and their operations have been carried on for a long time. This morning detectives visited the cemetery ground and arrested Robert Chewits, the Superintendent, and Andrew Mullen. The prisoners were this afternoon held in $5,000 each for a further hearing on Friday next.

When the body-snatchers were brought into court to-day, they narrowly escaped lynching at the hands of a mob, which gathered around the court. Robert Chew testified that he had been in the cemetery's employ eleven years. He received three dollars for each body taken from the cemetery. Body-snatching had been going on for nine years. His brother-in-law, Solomon Butcher, now in Maryland, did it first. Then a man named Myers and then McNamee. Sometimes, if the wagon came and the driver said they were short, the coffins were opened in the receiving vault, the corpse snatched, and the farce of burying the empty coffin was gone through with next day. The records of burials found at the cemetery this morning showed that in two months fifty-five bodies were in one grave. This created a sensation among the audience. As soon as the crowd outside of the Magistrate's office learned that the case was over, an overwhelming rush was made for the entry and the gateway, with threats to lynch the prisoners, and a Sergeant and ten of the reserves had to be sent for. The crowd made another rush, and men and women struck at the captives, who shrank and cowered before them. The policemen drew their clubs, and almost on a trot went down Chestnut street to the Central station, where the prisoners were locked up for the night.

More About the Ghouls of Philadelphia.
The Colored Population Wild With Excite- ment Over the Systematic Robbing of Lebanon Cemetery for a Number of Years.
OHIO BRINGS UP THE REAR, AS USUAL.
PHILADELPHIA, December 7.—Wild excitement was created by the disclosures made in the Press of the doings of the organized band of grave robbers who were arrested with six bodies in their possession, that had been taken from the graves in Lebanon Cemetery. Later in the morning, after the apprehension of McNamee, Pillet and Levi Chew, two more members of the gang, Andrew Mullen, alias "Yank," and Robert Chew, superintendent of the Lebanon Cemetery, were arrested. The prisoners, with the exception, of Mullen, who did not appear, having violated a parole granted him, were given a hearing before Magistrate Lennon and held in $5,000 bail each for a for a further hearing on Friday afternoon. An immense crowd of people surrounded the magistrate's office and threatened to kill the resurrectionists. A squad of police was sent for and by their aid the men were removed to a place of safety, although Razors and Revolvers were displayed. An indignation meeting of colored people will be held on Thursday in Liberty Hall. Of the six corpses captured five have been identified, as follows:

Mrs. Clara Ringgold, Eighteenth and Addison streets; Hans Jorgensen, 506 Hurst street; James Kennedy, 618 St. Mary street; Charles Robinson, 1320 Kates street; William Antonio, 308 Lombard street.

Lebanon Cemetery, a well-known burial ground for colored persons on Passgunk avenue, below Broad street, has been robbed of nearly all its dead by some ghouls, who have boldly plied their nefarious trade for the last nine years or more.

About eighteen months ago there was employed in Dooner's saloon (then at Eighth and Chestnut streets) a tall colored fellow, who every one knew by the name of "Jim." His full name was James Carson Wicks. When he died his body was placed beneath the sod of the Lebanon Cemetery. About a week after the interment a couple of young men were in Dooner's saloon, when one of them remarked to the proprietor: "I see poor Jim's gone." "Yes," replied Dooner, "he's been dead about a week." "He has," was the reply; "well. I've seen him within a couple of days." Then the young man laughed, winked his eye and walked out. After their departure the proprietor inquired who they were, and being informed that the men were students at the Jefferson medical College his

Suspicions were Aroused.

The clew was followed up, and it was soon found that the bodies of nearly all the colored persons who died in the fall, winter or spring, and whose remains were taken to Lebanon Cemetery, became eventually the subjects for the scalpel at Jefferson College, while those who were so fortunate as to die in warm weather, when medical colleges were not in session, were allowed to return to the dust in the ordinary way.

Going back a few years it seems there were three "boss body-snatchers, who confined their operations mostly in the Lebanon Cemetery. There were Sol. Butcher, a brother-in-law of the Chews, since deceased; John Mayer, a German saloon keeper, whose place was formerly at Tenth and Sansom streets, but who afterward kept on Germantown avenue, near, Oxford street, and is now in New York as a bartender. He was succeeded by Frank McNamee, an Eighth ward physician, who is also in the express business with the Philadelphia and Atlantic City Railroad, and who has for a few years past run a summer express to Bryn Mawr. His partners or employes were Henry Pillet, better known as "Dutch," a one-eyed, small, stout fellow; Levi Chew, a muscular, coal-black darkey, who was known as "Charcoal," and Andrew Mullen, a driver for McNamee, known as "Yank." They were assisted by Robert Charles McNamee, Pillet, Mullen and the two Chews were arrested. Robert was badly scared and tried to make a clean breast of the affair, but his various statements were so widely different that not much credence was given to them. A premium of $3 was paid for each body removed from the cemetery.

SEARCHING FOR THE DEAD.
the mournful work of searching for the dead in Lebanon Cemetery was systematically begun yesterday, and the investigation is to be patiently persisted in until it has been definitely ascertained how many bodies have found their way into the Jefferson pickling vats, and how many remain where loving hands laid them to rest. It was after 8 o'clock before the searchers began to arrive, and then in straggling groups of twos and threes, many of them carrying spades and shovels. The only persons in charge of the place were William Williams, the nephew of Levi Chew, and Lewis Williams, the grave-digger, and they refused to permit any one to begin digging until the arrival of some of the trustees. Guy M. Burton, the president of the Cemetery Company, arrived about 10 o'clock, and applications were at once made to him for permission to make the examinations. This was accorded to all persons holding permits from the board of health. The first thing done was the examination of the empty coffins, which had contained the corpses captured by the Press reporters. Five of the six were placed upon the wagon of Undertaker Dutier, to be taken to his establishment, to be repaired preparatory to receiving their former occupants for reinterment in the desecrated graves. This did not occupy more than two hours, and excited considerable curiosity among the spectators, many of whom imagined that it was the first discovery of the empty caskets.
By noon the character and extent of the crowd had changed visibly. There were about 100 blacks on the ground and as many whites. The latter were mainly made up of young men, boys and slatternly women, pushing and crowding about the grave-diggers the moment a spade was stuck in the ground. The boys played leap-frog over the tombstones, and the slip-shod women joked and bantered with the men. Grief was a subject of ridicule; the scoffers turned what should have been a solemn scene into one of vulgar mockery.

STEALING A SLIPPER.

Some of the behavior was simply disgraceful. H. Price Williams, the colored turnkey of the seventeenth district station-house, distinguished himself by getting into a fight with Guy Burton. When the empty coffins were placed in the undertaker's wagon the one in which had reposed the remains of Clara Ringgold was noticed to contain a white kid slipper. It had covered one of the feet of the dead woman, and had been tossed back into the grave after the ghouls had stripped the body. Williams saw the slipper, and, pushing his way through the crowd, he boldly thrust his hand into the coffin, and, taking it out, slipped it into his pocket. The action, quick as it was, did not escape detection. Williams was walking away from the wagon, when he was suddenly seized by the strong arm of Mr. Burton and commanded to give up the dead woman's property. With the most amazing assurance he refused point blank, whereupon Burton grasped him by the throat and choked him vigorously. Williams reached into his back pocket apparently to draw a weapon, but he was not quick enough, for in another instant he lay sprawling on his back. During the struggle the slipper was dropped on the ground, and was recovered and placed in the coffin. Williams did not appear at all ashamed of what he had done, but very coolly announced his intention of securing some sort of a relic, and started in search of a human bone, which he found, wrapped in a newspaper, and took away with him. While this was going on inside the cemetery two young women were having a regular set-two outside of the southern fence. The contest was witnessed by several men and boys, who clapped their hands loudly whenever one of the combatants succeeded in digging her finger-nails deep into the other's flesh. In another part of the grave-yard two youngsters amused themselves with a couple of thigh bones, which they had dug out of a shallow grave. Near the upper end of the fence, lying uncovered on the ground, was the disjointed skeleton of a human being. A colored man who had evidently been drinking came along, and, giving the skull a kick, sent it flying twenty yards away. It was picked up by a boy and tossed to a companion, and the two kept up their horrid sport until they tired of it.
A SINGULAR DISCOVERY

At 2 o'clock the grave of Josephine White, who was buried in September, 1881, was opened, and the noisy crowd were treated to a genuine sensation. The men dug steadily until a child's coffin was reached and the earth removed from around it. A rope was then slipped under the head and the coffin lifted to the surface. It contained the body of Florence Woodson, the niece of Josephine White, who had been buried in the same grave. The child's corpse had not been disturbed. The diggers went to work again, and after penetrating two feet deeper uncovered the coffin of an adult. The sticky soil was scraped from the plate, revealing instead of the name Josephine White, that of Elizabeth Given, aged 79 years, who died December 12, 1881! "My God," exclaimed a man standing on the grave's brink, "what does this mean? The body of my child is here! Where is Josephine White, my sister?"

"Perhaps," suggested a bystander, "this body has been buried in your lot without authority, and the body of your sister may be underneath. Dig deeper." After some little consideration the hint was acted upon, and again the men went to work. The coffin containing the corpse of Elizabeth Givin was lifted out of the grave, and the spades removed another foot of earth. A second coffin came to light, and this, instead of holding the corpse of Woodson's sister, covered the body of John Givin, an old man.

"Well," said Woodson when this startling discovery was made, "the thieving hounds were not satisfied with her body alone, they've taken coffin and all."

This was probably the case, as the presence of the child's body showed conclusively that there could have been no mistake in locating the grave. Following immediately after this was another and even more curious discovery. John Lymas, armed with a permit, had come to search for the body of his mother, Leah Lymas, who was buried April 14, 1881. The grave was opened, and three feet below the surface was found the battered name-plate belonging to Mrs. Lymas's coffin, but the coffin itself and its silent tenant had been stolen.

ROW IN THE THIRD WARD

the particulars of which, as far as could be ascertained, are about as follows:

About 4.30 o'clock, a number of colored men, in all about 15, came down Madison street toward Front, evidently coming from the Fifth Ward, for the purpose of seeing what was to be seen. They marched down the street in double file and appeared to be very peaceful. After they crossed Front street and proceeded out Maryland Avenue, in the direction of the Eleventh Ward, when the crowd around the Third Ward polls obstructed their progress and they were compelled to halt.

This was a signal among the rough element in that vicinity for a fight and they (the whites) started a row and one colored man was knocked down with a large stone, when a general fight ensued. The negroes soon fled and the officers endeavored to quiet the rioters, when they pounced upon officer Blackburn, took his club from him, jumped upon him and beat him, but he succeeded in capturing one of his assailants, after which the riot in a measure was stopped.

This state of affairs did not exist long, for the colored men feeling sore over the sudden attack, again came upon the scene with reinforcements, all of whom were armed with revolvers, and when at Second and Madison Sts., drawn their weapons and fired into the crowd several times, scattering them right and left. This action on the part of the colored men, took the men by surprise and it was a few minutes before they could recover from their surprise, when they made a raid on the colored men, who were about thirty strong, and routed them. They were followed by a howling crowd for several squares, when they succeeded in getting away.

THE WOUNDED.

At the time of the shooting the colored men emptied the chambers of their
revolvers. Many of the shots took effect as the crowd was a large one. MR BISHOP TALKS SENSIBLY.
So far as the result is personal to myself, I have no regrets, but I do regard the election of Gen Butler to the office of governor as a great calamity to the state of Massachusetts. In accounting for his success, we may say that a variety of causes have contributed to the result. Conspicuous among them all, and of great influence with a large class of conscientious citizens, is the disgust of the people with the notorious system of the assessment of office-holders for political purposes, a wrong for which the republicans of Massachusetts are, in a measure, responsible or chargeable, but for it the republican party of the country, in common with the democratic party, is responsible. There can also be reckoned among the moving causes of republican defeat in Massachusetts this fall, the wide-spread alarm stirred among the liquor dealers by the recent developments at the West, in favor of prohibition; and that has led them, no doubt, to form vigorous combinations, which have worked to the same result.

The republican party, in my opinion, is a party of advance, and not a party which can live upon a dead issue. Its policy should be distinctly identical with the reform of the civil service and with the most economical expenditure of the public money, both in the nation and in the state. It should be identified with a tariff sufficient to produce the necessary governmental revenue, and, at the same time, adjusted to the needs of the industries of the country. The republican party should be the party of reform and of progress, and should grasp the great and vital questions of the future with the same vigor and force which characterized it in its handling of the issues of the past. The administration of our state affairs has been, and is, most excellent. A thorough revision of salaries and expenditures, made a few years since, has placed the expenditures of the state on a most economical basis. The outcry for a change in the state administration, simply for the sake of change, is altogether without reason. No administration can ever excel that of Gov Long, in the faithfulness and care with which every detail is attended to, and in its thoroughly non-partisan character. The measures of that administration are taken, I believe, upon their merits alone, and all appointments to office are made on the sole ground of fitness. If there are better criterions by which to judge of the administration of state affairs, I have yet to find them. Gen Butler cannot have a successful administration in Massachusetts unless he imitates his predecessor in the points I have named. The best pattern Gov Butler can have for his guidance in discharging the duties of his office, is the man whom he succeeds. If he should imitate him, whatever of merit may attach to his administration will belong to another, and not to himself; and so far as he departs from the independent and non-partisan character of the present state government, he will introduce an administration of which Massachusetts will have no occasion to be proud.
