ACQUITTED OF RIOTING
THE JURY FIND GREENWOOD NOT GUILTY.
EDWARD CASSIDY ON TRIAL.
He is Found Guilty of Violating the Liquor Law by Selling Without a License. The Defendant has been Arrested.
At the session of court Lewis Woodland, Charles Moore and Alonzo Greenwood were arraigned for having been engaged in a riotous disturbance on election day. Woodland was not represented by counsel and pleaded guilty as charged. He was sentenced by Justice Houston to pay the costs of prosecution and a fine of $20. His Honor told Woodland that the penalty was fixed at the minimum allowed by law on account of the injury which the prisoner had received.

A jury was drawn to hear the evidence in the case of the other two defendants. Austin Harrington, Esq., counsel for Greenwood, asked to have the indictment quashed on the ground that it did not specify at what hour the alleged riot in which Greenwood took part occurred. He argued the point at some length, but his request was overruled by the court.

Moore, not being ready with his witnesses, by request of his counsel, Walter Bacon, Esq., a severance was granted and Greenwood's case was proceeded with.

John W. Carey told how a gang of about 20 negroes marched down Maryland avenue with clubs in their hands on election day with clubs in their hands on election day and after hustling the persons around the polls started a fight, but were dispersed. They were under the leadership of 4.30 o'clock in the afternoon. The night lasted about 10 minutes. Do not recognize the prisoner as one of the rioters.

Henry Witsil, sworn, corroborated Carey's testimony and said a number of persons ran into his store for safety. Did not see the prisoner.

John T. Dickey saw the 6 o'clock disturbance, but did not recognize the defendant.

Willian D. Hickman saw the crowd of colored men going toward the Third ward polls; heard firing and ran down to see what was the matter; saw Alonzo Greenwood in the crowd; am not mistaken, and have known the defendant some time; knew two or three men in the party.

John Allen said Greenwood told him the "boys" had had some fun and he, Allen, should have been along. When asked by Deputy Attorney Cooper whether Greenwood had been in the crowd Allen said no and added that because he, the witness, might say to Cooper "you ought to have been along the Brandywine, was no reason I was there." The fineness of the argument was apparent and created considerable merriment.

Spencer and Jane Greenwood, the father and mother of the prisoner, said their son was at home drunk from 2 o'clock in the afternoon until 11 o'clock at night. The former swore that Alonzo was in the house all the afternoon and evening and the latter vouched for the time from 7 to 11 p. m., having been absent during the afternoon. The defense rested. Deputy Attorney General Cooper and Mr. Harrington both made 20 minute addresses to the jury and Judge Houston charged them.

His Honor said the evidence was conflicting and of course if any doubt existed as to where the prisoner was at the time of the riot he should have the benefit of it.

A jurior asked if the fact of Greenwood being in the crowd made him a rioter. He was informed that if the assemblage was proven to have been a riotous one, Greenwood was as a member of it guilty of the offence charged.

The jury retired at 5.15, at 8 oclock returning with a verdict of not guilty. The defendant was therefore dismissed.

THIS MORNING'S SESSION.

At the opening of court this morning Charles Moore, charged with complicity in the election day riot, was discharged, the case having been abandoned at the instance of the Attorney-General, the result of the Greenwood jury case having prompted the action.

When the case of the State vs. Edward Cassidy was called, on the charge of violating the liquor law, the defendant's counsel, W. Bacon, Esq., moved for a continuance, owing to the absence of witnesses.

The Attorney-General said the case had been continued two or three times already at the instance of Cassidy's counsel, and he didn't think he was entitled to any more indulgence.
In the absence of Cassidy, who was held yesterday by Mayor Wales on a similar charge, the court decided to go on in the absence of the defendant, who was out on bail. A jury was drawn and the examination of witnesses was begun.

Emory Diety, colored, sworn: saw Cassidy, about the middle of October, at the northwest corner of Water and Shipley streets, sell liquor to Jacob Trusty; in the presence of Cassidy's wife; Trusty asked for liquor; Cassidy set out bottle and Trusty and I both took a drink of liquor and paid for it; paid 10 cents a drink; on Sunday Cassidy charged 10 cents and during the week 5 cents.

He struck the gentleman two on three severe blows with the piece of scantling, and was preparing to strike him again when Mr. Binford shot him twice in the back, and right arm, upon which he fell. Willis also broke the fingers of a Mr. Robert Simpson in the affray. The negro lived one hour after the shooting, and a post-mortem examination showed that one ball passed through the kidneys, the second through the liver, and the fourth shattered the bone in the right arm. It is thought this shot was fired by some other party, as the ball was smaller than those from Mr. Binford's pistol, which were of a thirty-two calibre. The coroner's jury rendered a verdict that the negro Willis Edwards came to his death by pistol shots fired by B. H. Binford in self-defence, and that the shooting was justifiable. Mr. Binford's injuries were quite severe. He suffered from two severe blows, one on the neck, and the other on the shoulder. The blow delivered on the neck was a slanting one, otherwise it would have killed him instantly.

Shot in Jail and Dies of His Wounds.
Just at the close of the last term of our Superior Court, Wilson Edwards, colored, of Sandy Ridge Township, was lodged in jail, for want of bondsmen, a peace warrant having been sworn out against him by a colored woman whom he had endeavored to shoot.

On Wednesday, when his dinner was sent up, he was found lying on the floor of his cell, without coat or shirt on, and sullenly refused to take his dinner. In an hour afterward, Sheriff Price went up and found him still lying on the floor, in a sullen mood, and in reply to the question as to why he didn't eat his dinner, used profane and abusive language. From this and other matters, Sheriff Price thought perhaps his mind was wrong, and that he had better be ironed before hurting himself or some one else. He sent off and procured the help of three or four stout colored men, but upon their arrival he was found to be in the notion of fighting, and threatened to kill any one who entered the cell; and being well armed with heavy stuff torn from the ceiling of his cell, he was rightly considered a dangerous customer. By this time, other help came, among them several white men—J. E. W. Austin, Jno. S. Richardson, B. H. Binford, E. T. wade, Rob't Simpson, and others—and as it was dangerous to go into the room where he was, he having all advantages, it was decided that it was best to open the door and allow him to come out, and overpower him, as he came. But it was found that he was harder to manage than they had anticipated, and he came so quick, with a stick in each hand, and his naked body so slick he could not be held, that he took the crowd somewhat by surprise, and began striking right and left with his murderous weapons. Ben. Blakeney, colored, was the first victim, he having been punched in the mouth with a stick, before the door was opened. Rob't Simpson next had two fingers broken. Berry H. Binford was next struck about the neck, and from this the negro's spite seemed to centre on Binford, and he followed him on across the passage into an opposite dungeon, where he "got in" another blow, which brought Mr. B. to the wall. Just here, three shots were fired, and though they entered the negro's body and two of them produced fatal wounds, he struggled on until forced to the floor by J. Richardson, who had swung to a handkerchief the negro had around his neck. After he was down, it was known that he was seriously hurt, and physicians were sent for, and Dr. Welsh soon came and said there was no chance to save him. In the meantime, Mr. Binford was taken to a room below and Dr. Ramsay called in, who found his patient badly hurt and suffering greatly from the blow on the side of the neck and shoulder. Had this blow been otherwise than a glancing one, Binford would, in all probability, have been instantly killed.

The negro died in less than an hour—one ball having passed through the liver, a second just above, while a third went through the kidney.

Afterwards, a former fellow-prisoner who was taken from the cell only a few days ago, told Sheriff Price that the prisoner, Edwards, had disclosed to him a plan he had formed to escape, which was to "play off crazy," and should Sheriff A. J. Price come alone and open the door he would brain him and rush out. Should the Sheriff come with help he would fight his way through and escape or be killed in the attempt. He was a powerful, well muscled, able-bodied negro 30 or 35 years old, and was known as a desperate character. The affair of course is to be greatly regretted but no blame can be attached to any one, as it was necessary to iron him if possible or he would have torn up the jail and come out, and after the effort was made it became necessary to fire on him or he would have killed others.

Since Edwards had been jailed, conclusive evidence has been brought out, showing that he was the person who shot Jack Huneycutt, col'd, some time ago, in Sandy Ridge Township, mention of which was made in this paper at the time.

The coroner's jury returned a verdict that the killing was in self-defense and justifiable.—Monroe Enquirer.

Frankfort-on-the-Main, containing a population of about 100,000, is said to be the richest city of its size in the world. If its wealth were equally divided among the inhabitants, every man, woman and child would have, it is said, some $4,000 apiece. There are, as may be supposed, many poor people in the town; but the citizens are, as a whole, in unusually comfortable circumstances—more so, probably, than the citizens of any other capital in Germany or Europe. It is stated that there are 100 Frankforters worth from $4,000,000 to $7,000,000 each, and 250 who are worth $3,000,000 and upward. The city is one of the great banking centres of the globe. Its aggregate banking capital is estimated at $2,000,000,000, more than one-fourth of which the famous Rothschilds—whose original and parent house is there—own and control. The annual transactions in bills of exchange are in excess of $100,000,000.

A TEST FOR INSANITY.—Dr. Lamson will not have died in vain if the suggestion made by one of the British authorities on insanity is hereafter applied to test the perceptive faculties of alleged insane murderers. The suggestion is that a red hot poker be handed to the said alleged insane person; if he takes it, he is to be adjudged as really unable to distinguish between right and wrong; but if he refuses it, then he is to he considered as responsible and be made to suffer accordingly. The test is a very simple one, and there seems to be no reason why it should not be accepted as satisfactory. He who can remember that a red hot poker burns can also remember to kill another is a crime.—London Graphic.

The opening of the Western North Carolina Railroad from Asheville to Warm Springs, and the quick connection arrangements with the Tennessee railroads, are beginning to effect a revolution in travel east and west. Pullman sleepers are put on at Greensboro. At Henry passengers going west get breakfast, and then take seats in an observation car, from whence they get views of the grand scenery all the way from Henry's to Warm Springs.

There was a man in Flint, Michigan, last week with a patent lock for sale, and to demonstrate its superiority over all others, he would pick any kind of a lock in a few seconds. A Sheriff put him in irons to test his ability, and he unlocked the handcuffs and shackles with a small piece of iron as soon as the officer could have done it with the keys. He was so expert that the Mayor and Marshal forbid his giving public exhibitions of lock picking.

THE Universal Peace Union convened in Washington on the 28th.

EIGHT prisoners, including two murderers and one highway robber, effected their escape from the jail at Tuscaloosa, Ala., on the 27th, by cutting the hinges off the cell door and running over the jailer.

THE Governor of Michigan has ordered an investigation into the truth of affidavits charging N. Delong, Mayor of Muskegon, with attempting to bribe an Alderman to vote for one of his nominees to office.

A. F. BRACKMAN, who for some weeks was the laughing-stock of St. Louis, died the other day in the Missouri Insane Asylum. He came from Nebraska with an abundance of money, married a chambermaid at the Planters' House, gave her a wardrobe costing $1,500, and was deserted on the day succeeding the wedding. He was several times arrested for eccentric conduct on the streets. An autopsy revealed the fact that he died from softening of the brain.

WILLIAM A. HALL, the thieving Assistant Auditor of Newark, N. J., has been captured at Toronto. He spent three months at Prescott, where he kept two fast horses and carried a large amount in diamonds. He is said to have secured $40,000 in plunder.
JOHN C. WOLCOTT, the best-known lawyer in Western Massachusetts, has been jailed in Boston to make him sober. Then he will be arraigned in the federal court for charging a pensioner $100 for prosecuting his claim.

BRAVE BEAR, the Sioux Indian who would have been executed on the 9th of March for the murder of a soldier named Johnson, near Fort Sully, Dak., but for an appeal to the Supreme Court and motion for a new trial, has been resentenced to be hanged on the 20th of July, the Supreme Court having denied him a trial. He fully deserves the sentence, as he is clearly guilty not only of this murder, but of others, including an entire white family near Pembina. Upon being asked if he had anything to say before being sentenced, Brave Bear replied: "I have taken the white man's part always. I am disappointed at the treatment of the white man. They can do as they please with me, and cut me to pieces if they choose." So saying he received the sentence with the utmost unconcern.

At Springfield, Ohio, May 29, a man named Kitzmiller, becoming enraged at his daughter for keeping company with a man of whom he disapproved, drew a revolver and shot her dead. He narrowly escaped lynching at the hands of his neighbors before he was taken to jail.

MARCUS DE BASTIDE, a young French Canadian, was assaulted by members of the congregation of the French Canadian Catholic chapel in New York City, May 28. The cause of the assault was the distribution by Bastide of tracts printed in French calculated to persuade people to accept Protestant beliefs. He had attended services at the chapel and the officiating clergyman denounced his books to the congregation.

A COLLISION between trackmen of the Denver & New Orleans and Denver & Rio Grande roads occurred near Denver, Colo., May 28. The latter road undertook to block the progress of the former by running an empty engine under a full head of steam into a gang of men laying the track at a crossing. None of the men were injured, but the engine was derailed and plowed up the track for a considerable distance.

WILLIS EDWARDS, a notorious desperado, was killed in the jail at Monroe Court-house, N. C., the other day, in an affray with the Sheriff and his posse. Edwards succeeded in severely wounding the four men who attempted to subdue him.

FRANK MILLER, while robbing the residence of H. P. Moore at Erie, Pa., the other night, was nearly beheaded with a scythe.

The Attorney-General has decided that Secretary Kirkwood is not eligible for appointment on the Tariff Commission.

F. H. STONER and Arthur J. Cole, of Chicago, were drowned, May 27, by the cap-sizing of a boat.

ALF. BURNETT committed suicide at Topeka, Kans., on the 28th, by shooting himself in the temple. He had been released from the County Jail the day before, having served out a sentence of thirty days for selling liquor without a license.

A NUMBER of Dunkards assembled in Eapho Township, Lancaster County, Pa., a few days ago for the purpose of raising the framework of a meeting-house. The lower story and about one-half of the second story had already been successfully put together, and between forty and fifty persons were standing on some jolsts on the second story on the unfinished part of the building, placing the rafters in position. There was a span of forty or fifty feet, and over this had been stretched some girders, upon which these persons were standing. They worked without accident until between 9 and 10 o'clock in the morning, when, with a loud crash, the timbers broke and fell, carrying their living freight with them. ROCHEPORT. Mo., April 8 — Twenty or 1
ROCHEPORT, Mo., April 8. — Twenty or more drunken negroes created a disturbance on the street late on Saturday night, and assaulted several white men, whereupon special deputies were sworn in to preserve the peace. One of the rioters attempted to strike an officer, who drew a revolver and fired at his assailant, but without hitting him. The negroes then fled, but later, while 15 or 20 men and boys were standing on the street, returned and fired a volley from guns and pistols from an alley on the opposite side of the street. Eight of the party were wounded, but none seriously. Great excitement ensued, and ten of the negroes were arrested.

Kansas City, April 3.—The news of the killing of Jesse James created an immense sensation in this city, although the report was generally treated with discredit and even at this late hour many unbelievers can be found. This afternoon as soon as the news was received here Police Commissioner Craig left for St. Joseph with a heavily armed posse of men to guard the body of James and furnish protection for the man who killed him. At the station house it was learned that a young man who has been hanging about the station for several weeks past, was the person who shot and killed Jesse James. Ford left this city about a week since and joined James in the vicinity of St. Joseph, remaining with him until an opportunity to kill him was found. From the police it is learned that Ford, who is said to be a member of the gang, was under control of Craig, and has been used as an instrument for James' destruction. Ford is a young man about twenty-two years of age, and looked like a verdant from the country. In appearance he is a mere boy, and is the last person in the world to be taken for the slayer of an outlaw. The Oregon Short Line. Omaha, Neb., April 3.—The report is telegraphed from Sioux City that the Union Pacific had determined to abandon all work on the Oregon Short Line is without any foundation whatever. Assistant General Manager Kemball, of the Union Pacific, says that every nerve is being strained to push the Oregon Short Line as rapidly as possible. The track has been laid within eight miles of Snake river, Montana. The bridge across Snake river will be in position in a few weeks, and a large grading force will soon commence work on the west side of the Snake river and from there to Wood river and Boise City, Idaho, work will be rapidly rushed forward. Steel rails have been contracted for and are being rooled and shipped to the front. It is expected this season to grade to Boise City and to lay between three and four hundred miles of track. Riotous Negroes.
St. Louis, Mo., April 3.—A Republican's Rockport, Mo., special says: Some twenty or more drunken negroes created a disturbance on the street last night, and assaulted one or two white men. Several special deputies were sworn in to maintain order, who notified the negroes that they must disperse or be arrested. One of them attempted to strike one of the officers, who drew a weapon and fired at his assailant without hitting him. The negroes then fled, but some were taken, and while some fifteen or twenty men and boys were standing on the street talking together a volley from guns and pistols was fired at them by negroes from an alley on the opposite side of the street, and one of them wounded, but none seriously. Great excitement ensued, and ten of the negroes were arrested and locked up.

Killing of a Bad Man.

Nashville, Tenn., April 3.—An American's Murfreesboro special says: O'Brien, a special deputy sheriff, went out last night to arrest Bethel Thompson, who shot an officer in Shelbyville last year when about to be arrested for horse stealing. Thompson was concealing himself at a house of ill-fame and was found in bed. While O'Brien was reading his warrant Thompson shot him with a pistol which he drew from under his pillow, the bullet passing through the neck, inflicting a bad and probably fata' wound. O'Brien returned the fire, killing Thompson instantly. Thompson was the third man O'Brien has killed.

Stabbed by a Companion.

St. Louis, April 3.—A special to the Republican says: While Charles Fisher and a man named Trotter were riding side by side on horse-back near Poplin station, on the Cairo branch of the Iron Mountain railway, yesterday afternoon, they got into yn altercation about some business transaction, and Trotter drew a knife and stabbed Fisher to the heart, killing him. Trotter was arrested. There was great excitement and threats of lynching him were freely made by Fisher's friends.

Mrs. Mackey, who is in Paris, denies the reported engagement of her daughter to Don Philippe de Bourbon.

St. Paul and Winnipeg dispatches record heavy snow storms along the Canadian Pacific, which block traveling until warm weather. The storm at Winnipeg was unprecedentedly severe. At St. James, Mo., the other day, J. R. Bowman, late Judge of Phelps County, fired a load of buckshot into the body of Alfred Hayes.

J. W. Kerr, until recently paying teller of the Bank of the Republic, Washington, killed himself on the 29th. He left a note, saying: "Realizing that I have expended money belonging to others to an extent that I can never repay, I have sought this relief from dishonor, sorrow and disgrace."

JOHN KENNEDY and John O'Neal, carpenters, fell from a scaffolding in Denver, Colo., March 30, and were precipitated a distance of seventy-five feet. Kennedy will probably recover. O'Neal is a native of Prince Edward Island, where he has a wife. He will probably die from his injuries.

During a fire which destroyed several frame buildings in Le Sueur, Minn., on the 30th, Miss Fishbaum was burned to death, and another girl was slightly hurt by jumping from a window.

EX-GOVERNOR MOSES, of South Carolina, has again been arrested in New York on a charge of swindling.

ALLEN Fox, a wealthy citizen of Louisville, Ky., aged 81 years, mortally wounded himself with a razor the other evening.

TRUMAN DUNHAM, President of the Cleveland Linseed Oil Works, an old and honored citizen, was caught in machinery, March 30, and killed. He was alone in the basement, where there was a large belt which runs the grinder; in some unknown way he was caught in the belt, carried into the machinery and the body shockingly crushed. Deceased had been trustee of the Cleveland water-works for many years.

J. W. SHEEHAN, a young man stopping at the Metropolitan Hotel, Kansas City, Mo., was found dead in his room, March 30, having taken poison. The following note was found on the table: "My father's address is William Sheehan, North Walpole, N. H." Sheehan had a letter of recommendation from the Smith Refrigerator Manufacturing Company, of Michigan City, Ind., speaking of him as a sober, industrious man. It is supposed he took the dose in a fit of despondency, finding himself out of work and among strangers.

Two inmates of the Dayton (Ohio) Lunatic Asylum had a deadly struggle the other night. One, named John Drummond, had arrived that day. He was a farmer, living in Brown county, and the cause of his insanity was said to be jealousy. He had several times attempted suicide, and threatened to kill others. On his arrival he was quiet and tractable, but during the night he became noisy and was removed to a strong cell, in which was an old man named O'Connell, of quiet habit. When the watchman entered the cell, toward morning, O'Connell bounded out from the corner; frantic with excitement. He said Drummond had attacked and bitten him, so he choked him quiet. Drummond was found dead on the floor covered with blood, one eye gouged out and otherwise terribly mutilated. O'Connell was also badly bruised and scratched in many places, and one finger was nearly bitten off.

The reaper and mower trade is dull in Richmond, for the reason that our dealers have sold out all the stock they had on hand. The demand was large.

The brick work on Jo. Sanderson's new business house is progressing finely, and if the workmen could have suitable weather, it would soon be finished.

Harvesters are making things rattle this week between showers. If we could only have a week of settled weather the wheat would all be nicely cut and shocked and some of it stacked.

Rev. Dr. Flack, of Excelsior, was in the city on Friday night last. He is a very pleasant gentleman and by his energy and zeal has built up a considerable town at Excelsior.

Mr. Jas. A. Tuttle has sold his saddle and harness shop in this city to Mr. Hudgins, who will continue the business at the old stand on west side of the square. If he advertises his business well he will make money.

"The lips which touch liquor shall never touch mine," is a good motto for young women to adopt, and having once adopted it stick to it. We would say to a young lady, contemplating matrimony, never marry a man if he gets drunk. Better get into your coffin, pull the lid down and be buried alive than to marry a man who gets drunk, as your torture will be less and you will be the quicker out of your misery. There are now in this world too many broken, crushed, disheatened wives with poor, pithless, worthless, drunken husbands who make of home a hell. Too many weak, worn, wicked, worthless wrecks who love liquor for the opportunity that it give them to get away on drunks, associate with other loafers, dirty their garments and wallow in the gutter. If you do not wish to get into a coffin, tie a piece of stinking meat in your bosom so you will always have it there to smell of and to rub up against you, and you will be as happy and contented as you ever can be with a droozling, slobbering mumbling, grumbling, incoherent, gutter-seeking wretch of humanity for a husband, or rather for a dead-weight or disgrace—that is if you are sensitive in your nature. We have seen and been acquainted with many wives of drunken husbands but never yet saw a happy one.
